screens.title: Transactions and Error Handling
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will learn what a database transaction is and why it is central to data integrity. A transaction groups related updates so they succeed or fail as a single unit. That all-or-nothing guarantee prevents partial updates that corrupt state. You will also learn the ACID principles — Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — as concise rules you can apply when designing updates in Python. We will practice committing and rolling back transactions, use try-except blocks to catch database errors, and adopt context managers to reduce boilerplate and avoid leaving connections open. A concrete running example is a simulated bank transfer between two accounts: we will show balances before and after, perform a debit and a credit, and simulate an error to force a rollback. Finally, you will get a short checklist of common mistakes to avoid in production: forgetting to commit, catching errors too broadly, and keeping transactions longer than necessary. By the end you will understand how to protect data correctness and handle errors that commonly occur in real applications.

screens.title: What is a Transaction?
screens.narratorSegment: A transaction is a single logical unit of work that groups multiple database operations so they succeed or fail together. Think of a bank transfer: the system must debit one account and credit another. If the debit succeeds but the credit fails, the money disappears unless both updates are treated as a single unit. That is atomicity — an entire transaction must complete as a whole. Transactions also ensure the database moves from one valid state to another; constraints and validations must hold before and after. A concrete example you will use in the lab is debiting Alice and crediting Bob in the same transaction, then deliberately raising an error to see rollback undo both operations. A common misconception is that individual S Q L statements are automatically safe; they are not when multiple related statements must be consistent together. Finally, a practical rule: keep each transaction focused and short. Long transactions hold locks for longer, increasing contention. What part of a multi-step update would you group into a single transaction in your application? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A transaction groups related operations into an atomic unit so either all succeed or all fail, preventing partial updates.

content.html:
Core Concept
What is a Transaction?
A transaction groups one or more operations so they succeed or fail together.

Concrete example: Transfer $200 from Alice to Bob. Debit then credit must both complete.

Misconception: Individual statements are not a substitute for transactions when several updates must be consistent.

Why it matters: Prevents partial updates that corrupt balances or violate constraints.

Key Takeaway

Group logically related updates in a single transaction to guarantee all-or-nothing behavior.

Bank Transfer — annotated steps
1. Begin transaction (implicit after connect)
2. Check sender balance and constraints
3. Update sender balance (debit)
4. Update receiver balance (credit) — commit if all OK
If step 4 fails, rollback will undo step 3 so both debit and credit are reversed. This preserves atomicity and consistency.

screens.title: ACID Properties Explained
screens.narratorSegment: ACID is the shorthand for four properties that make transactions reliable. Atomicity ensures the transaction behaves as a single unit: either everything inside it happens or nothing does. Consistency means the database moves from one valid state to another, obeying constraints like unique keys and foreign keys. Isolation prevents a transaction's intermediate state from being visible to other concurrent transactions; the effect should be as if transactions ran one after another. Durability guarantees that once you commit, changes survive crashes. For example, if you commit a transfer and then power fails, durability means the committed balances remain when the database restarts. A frequent error is assuming isolation removes the need to validate inputs; isolation only controls visibility and ordering, not business rules. Another misconception is that durability removes the need to back up data; durability applies to committed changes, but backups and replication are still important operational practices. Consider a transfer: atomicity protects against half-applied updates, consistency enforces valid balances, isolation protects concurrent reads, and durability keeps the committed change even after failures. How will you verify each property in a test scenario?

keyIdea.title: ACID summary
keyIdea.text: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability collectively ensure reliable, isolated, and permanent transaction processing.

content.html:
Core Concept
ACID Properties
Atomicity: All operations inside a transaction succeed or all are undone.
Consistency: The database remains valid according to constraints and rules after the transaction.
Isolation: Transactions appear to run serially, preventing visibility of partial state.
Durability: Once committed, changes persist through system failures.
Example

Transfer test: confirm balances before, attempt transfer, and check that after a forced error the pre-transaction balances are restored.

Quick checks to validate each property
  • Atomicity: cause an error mid-transaction and ensure no partial writes remain.
  • Consistency: check constraints both before and after transactions.
  • Isolation: run concurrent reads during a long transaction to check visibility.
  • Durability: commit, simulate crash, restart, and verify committed rows persist.
Misconception check: isolation does not guarantee your business logic is correct — still validate inputs and balances explicitly.

screens.title: Commit and Rollback in Python
screens.narratorSegment: In Python database code, conn. commit() finalizes the active transaction and makes its changes permanent. conn. rollback() undoes all changes made in the current transaction, returning the database to the state before that transaction began. A typical pattern is to begin a transaction implicitly on connect, run a sequence of DML statements, then call commit if everything succeeds. If any exception is raised, the except block calls rollback. A concrete example is updating two account balances: after the debit and credit statements, commit makes the new balances durable. If the credit statement fails because of a constraint or a simulated application error, rollback ensures the debit is undone so the sender is not charged for a failed transfer. A common misunderstanding is that commit is automatic; many drivers start a transaction implicitly but require an explicit commit to persist DML changes. Always test by printing balances before and after commit or rollback so you can see the effect in practice. In practical terms, how conn.commit() and conn.rollback() control persistence. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Commit vs Rollback
keyIdea.text: Commit makes changes permanent; rollback undoes all changes in the active transaction. Use try-except to decide which to call.

content.html:
Definition
Commit and Rollback
Commit writes all pending changes to durable storage. Rollback undoes the current transaction. Use them to decide whether a multi-step operation becomes permanent.
# After DML operations
try:
  conn.commit()  # finalize
except Exception:
  conn.rollback()  # undo on error
Key Takeaway

Always call commit to persist DML, and rollback on error to avoid partial state.

Practical example: confirm effect
Print balances before transaction
Perform debit and credit statements
If error occurs, call conn.rollback()
If all good, call conn.commit()
Misconception check: Some drivers auto-commit by default for each statement; rely on driver docs and explicit commits for predictable behavior.

keyIdea.title: Walkthrough insight
keyIdea.text: Apply commit and rollback around related updates and observe the database before and after to verify behavior.

content.html:
Process Flow
Transfer: success and rollback paths
Follow these numbered actions to confirm transactional behavior and rollback effects.
1. Setup: CREATE TABLE and INSERT initial accounts, then conn.commit()
2. Start transfer: implicit transaction begins after setup
3. Debit sender: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - ?
4. Simulate error or have credit fail → except block calls conn.rollback()
5. If no error, perform credit and call conn.commit()
Code excerpt (escaped)
import sqlite3
conn = sqlite3.connect('transactions_example.db')
cursor = conn.cursor()
# setup and commit
cursor.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS accounts (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, balance REAL)")
cursor.execute("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO accounts (id,name,balance) VALUES (1,'Alice',1000.0)")
cursor.execute("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO accounts (id,name,balance) VALUES (2,'Bob',500.0)")
conn.commit()
# transfer
try:
  cursor.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - ? WHERE id = ?", (200,1))
  # simulate error here to force rollback
  cursor.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + ? WHERE id = ?", (200,2))
  conn.commit()
except sqlite3.Error:
  conn.rollback()
Tip: print balances before and after each run to confirm whether the commit or rollback took effect.

screens.title: Robust Error Handling Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Robust error handling prevents crashes and helps you decide whether to retry, rollback, or fail gracefully. The best practice is to catch specific database exception classes before falling back to broader handlers. For SQLite the chapter uses sqlite3. IntegrityError to detect constraint violations like duplicate keys. By handling IntegrityError you can provide a user-friendly message while leaving other errors to more general handlers. The pattern is try: perform updates and commit; except IntegrityError: rollback and inform the caller about the constraint; except sqlite3. Error: rollback and report a database problem for operational attention; except Exception: rollback and treat as unexpected. A common pitfall is catching Exception too broadly, which can hide programming errors that should be fixed. Another is forgetting to call rollback in each except branch; always ensure rollback runs when any error occurs during a transaction. Logging details while returning a clear message is a useful middle ground between silence and overwhelming stack traces. keyIdea.text: Catch specific database exceptions first, call rollback on error, log details, and report user-friendly messages when appropriate.

content.html:
Definition
Robust Error Handling
Handle known database errors explicitly and ensure rollback when any error occurs during a transaction.
Pattern: try → commit; except SpecificError → rollback; except DBError → rollback; except Exception → rollback.
Example: sqlite3.IntegrityError for unique constraint violations.
Example handler
try:
  # perform updates
  conn.commit()
except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e:
  conn.rollback()
  # user-friendly message about duplicate or constraint
except sqlite3.Error as e:
  conn.rollback()
  # operational DB error handling
except Exception as e:
  conn.rollback()
  # unexpected error
Misconception check: catching Exception hides programming bugs. Reserve broad handlers for logging and cleanup, not business logic.

screens.title: Context Managers for Transactions
screens.narratorSegment: Context managers simplify transaction management by automatically committing on successful exit and rolling back on exception. In the chapter we use sqlite3. connect as a context manager: when you open a connection with with sqlite3. connect(db_file) as conn, the block will commit if nothing went wrong, or rollback if an exception is raised. This reduces boilerplate and makes it less likely to forget commit or rollback. It also helps with closing resources: the connection is closed when the block exits. For other drivers like psycopg2, you may need to use the driver's context manager conventions for the connection and cursor. A practical example is wrapping the entire transfer operation inside a with block: set up the table and seed data outside or inside its own with block, then run the transfer in another with. A misconception is assuming all drivers implement the same with semantics; always confirm the driver behavior and test that an exception will trigger rollback as you expect. Would your code be clearer if you used context managers for both connection and cursor? Process Flow
Context Managers
Use the with-statement to reduce transaction boilerplate and ensure automatic commit or rollback.
Wrap a set of operations in with sqlite3.connect(db): the block commits on success, rolls back on exceptions, and closes the connection at exit.
For complex drivers, use their recommended context managers for connections and cursors.
Pro Tip

Use with wherever your driver supports it to avoid forgotten commits and leaked connections.

Code pattern
with sqlite3.connect('bank.db') as conn:
  cursor = conn.cursor()
  # DML here
  # commit happens automatically on block exit
Remember to test that exceptions inside the with block trigger rollback in your environment.

screens.title: Common Transaction Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: This screen lists common mistakes and the practical fixes you should apply. First, forgetting commit: changes appear local and disappear after the connection closes; the fix is to call conn. commit() when the transaction completes or use a with block. Second, not handling exceptions: unhandled errors cause crashes and leave the application in an unstable state; wrap DML in try-except and rollback on error. Third, catching Exception too broadly: this hides bugs and makes debugging harder; catch specific database exceptions first then use a generic handler for unexpected issues. Fourth, not closing connections: leaked connections exhaust resources; initialize conn = None, check if conn before closing, or use with to guarantee cleanup. Finally, long transactions and poor lock ordering can increase the risk of deadlocks; keep transactions short and design a consistent lock acquisition order. For each mistake the screen shows an actionable fix you can apply immediately in code or operations. Common Transaction Mistakes means don't forget commit, handle exceptions intentionally, avoid broad exception catches, close connections, and keep transactions short to reduce contention.. import sqlite3

db_file = 'bank.db'

conn = None

  conn = sqlite3.connect(db_file)
  cursor = conn.cursor()
  cursor.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS accounts (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, balance REAL NOT NULL)")
  cursor.execute("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO accounts (id, name, balance) VALUES (1, 'Alice', 1000.00)")
  cursor.execute("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO accounts (id, name, balance) VALUES (2, 'Bob', 500.00)")

  # TODO: implement display_balances and transfer_funds as next steps
except sqlite3.Error as e:
  print('Initial database setup error:', e)
finally:
  if conn:
    conn.close()

Bank Transfer Lab — Transfer logic
Use the template below. Replace TODOs with the checks and simulated error to test rollback behavior.
def transfer_funds(conn, sender_id, receiver_id, amount):
  cursor = conn.cursor()
  try:
    # TODO: select sender balance
    cursor.execute("SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = ?", (sender_id,))
    sender_balance = cursor.fetchone()[0]

    if sender_balance < amount:
      raise ValueError(f"Insufficient funds for account {sender_id}")

    # Debit sender
    cursor.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - ? WHERE id = ?", (amount, sender_id))
    print(f"Debited {amount} from account {sender_id}.")

    # TODO: simulate error for rollback test (uncomment to test)
    # if receiver_id == 999:

    # Credit receiver
    cursor.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + ? WHERE id = ?", (amount, receiver_id))

    print('Transaction successful!')

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will learn what a database transaction is and why it is central to data integrity. A transaction groups related updates so they succeed or fail as a single unit. That all-or-nothing guarantee prevents partial updates that corrupt state. You will also learn the ACID principles — Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — as concise rules you can apply when designing updates in Python. We will practice committing and rolling back transactions, use try-except blocks to catch database errors, and adopt context managers to reduce boilerplate and avoid leaving connections open. A concrete running example is a simulated bank transfer between two accounts: we will show balances before and after, perform a debit and a credit, and simulate an error to force a rollback. Finally, you will get a short checklist of common mistakes to avoid in production: forgetting to commit, catching errors too broadly, and keeping transactions longer than necessary. By the end you will understand how to protect data correctness and handle errors that commonly occur in real applications.

In this first set of objectives we focus on foundational understanding and practical control. You will learn to explain the ACID properties — what atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability mean for application code. You will practice committing and rolling back changes from Python so you can make updates permanent only when they are safe. The exercises emphasize clear examples: a bank transfer where both debit and credit must succeed or the whole transfer is undone. You will also learn to catch the right database exceptions, using specific exception classes before falling back to a general handler. That helps you present clearer error messages and avoid masking bugs. Each objective is paired with a simple mnemonic to help you remember when to commit, when to rollback, and which exceptions to catch. These skills reduce data corruption risk in single- and multi-step updates and prepare you for the hands-on bank transfer activity later in the chapter.

In this second set of objectives we focus on applied practice and avoidance of common pitfalls. You will implement a small bank transfer script that demonstrates a full transaction lifecycle including deliberate error simulation to trigger rollback. You will learn to initialize connections safely, checking for a non-null connection before attempting to close it, and to use explicit initialization like conn = None to avoid cleanup errors. You will practice diagnostic logging in except blocks so you can report constraint violations and permission errors clearly. Finally, you will identify transaction-level problems such as long-running transactions and lock ordering that can increase deadlock risk; the practical takeaway is to keep transactions short and simple. Each objective includes a quick mnemonic or micro-check to help you remember safe patterns while writing production-ready code.

A transaction is a single logical unit of work that groups multiple database operations so they succeed or fail together. Think of a bank transfer: the system must debit one account and credit another. If the debit succeeds but the credit fails, the money disappears unless both updates are treated as a single unit. That is atomicity — an entire transaction must complete as a whole. Transactions also ensure the database moves from one valid state to another; constraints and validations must hold before and after. A concrete example you will use in the lab is debiting Alice and crediting Bob in the same transaction, then deliberately raising an error to see rollback undo both operations. A common misconception is that individual S Q L statements are automatically safe; they are not when multiple related statements must be consistent together. Finally, a practical rule: keep each transaction focused and short. Long transactions hold locks for longer, increasing contention. What part of a multi-step update would you group into a single transaction in your application? ACID is the shorthand for four properties that make transactions reliable. Atomicity ensures the transaction behaves as a single unit: either everything inside it happens or nothing does. Consistency means the database moves from one valid state to another, obeying constraints like unique keys and foreign keys. Isolation prevents a transaction's intermediate state from being visible to other concurrent transactions; the effect should be as if transactions ran one after another. Durability guarantees that once you commit, changes survive crashes. For example, if you commit a transfer and then power fails, durability means the committed balances remain when the database restarts. A frequent error is assuming isolation removes the need to validate inputs; isolation only controls visibility and ordering, not business rules. Another misconception is that durability removes the need to back up data; durability applies to committed changes, but backups and replication are still important operational practices. Consider a transfer: atomicity protects against half-applied updates, consistency enforces valid balances, isolation protects concurrent reads, and durability keeps the committed change even after failures. How will you verify each property in a test scenario?

In Python database code, conn. commit() finalizes the active transaction and makes its changes permanent. conn. rollback() undoes all changes made in the current transaction, returning the database to the state before that transaction began. A typical pattern is to begin a transaction implicitly on connect, run a sequence of DML statements, then call commit if everything succeeds. If any exception is raised, the except block calls rollback. A concrete example is updating two account balances: after the debit and credit statements, commit makes the new balances durable. If the credit statement fails because of a constraint or a simulated application error, rollback ensures the debit is undone so the sender is not charged for a failed transfer. A common misunderstanding is that commit is automatic; many drivers start a transaction implicitly but require an explicit commit to persist DML changes. Always test by printing balances before and after commit or rollback so you can see the effect in practice.
